newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Nazi slaves want end to IG Farben, compensation.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi slaves want end to IG Farben, compensation.

text.p: German groups representing former slave workers sold by the Nazis to the notorious chemicals giant IG Farben demanded compensation on Wednesday from a final liquidation of the firm's assets.

"The murderous firm IG Farben, whose shares are soaked with the blood of tens of thousands, must be immediately dissolved and its victims compensated," Axel Koehler-Schnura, spokesman for the "Never Again" campaign, told journalists in Bonn.

IG Farben was the world's fourth-largest company until the end of World War Two and bought concentration camp prisoners from the Nazis to work in forced labour camps -- the largest of which was part of the Auschwitz concentration camp complex.

Koehler-Schnura, whose group represents survivors and relatives of victims of the Nazi regime, said it was scandalous that IG Farben, which produced Zyklon B gas for the Nazis' death camps, still existed.
"It is a scandal that shareholders are still receiving dividends while survivors get nothing," said Koehler-Schnura.

Henry Mathews, head of the Association of Critical Shareholders, said his group hoped to add resolutions to the agenda at this year's IG Farben shareholders' meeting on August 22 calling for the company's final liquidation.
IG Farben was split up after the war into BASF AG, Bayer AG and Hoechst AG, but a shell company, IG Farben in Liquidation, still exists to group outstanding asset claims.

The liquidation has been taking so long because of the company's ongoing fight to reclaim assets seized at the end of the war, above all property in east Germany which was nationalised by Soviet occupiers and which IG Farben was not able to try to reclaim until after German unification in 1990.

Mathews said there was no chance a majority of shareholders would back the final liquidation of the remaining 30 million marks of IG Farben assets, but he hoped at least five percent would support the motion and show moral support for survivors.
Peter Gingold, spokesman of the Association of Victims of the Nazi Regime, who lost most of his family in concentration camps, said financial compensation was not the main issue.
"Many of the survivors are in former eastern Europe and are ill, old and poor. It's not just the money they want but the recognition that they were slave workers," Gingold said.

IG Farben in Liquidation paid 30 million marks ($20 million) in compensation to the Jewish Claims Conference in 1957, but no compensation has been paid on an individual basis, or to any ex-slaves in eastern Europe.
